column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
Article gives the length as 76 miles (122 km); the entry says about 120 km, so no length is restated. Pollution rankings (2023 report) left out under the present-day rule.

Article says he graduated from the military school in 1963 but was part of La Tandona, the class of 1966: graduation year left out. Entry calls the body he presided over the Constituent Assembly; article calls it the Legislative Assembly: the text names neither office, saying only 'the assembly'. His presidency of it (1982-1983) is in the entry.

Entry dates the death of the last Changamire to about 1836; the article says Chirisamhuru was killed around 1835. No year is given for his death in the text. Article dates the state c. 1683-1866; the entry says it collapsed after about 1836. The text gives the Ndebele conquest around 1838 and Tohwechipi's surrender in 1866 as the article does, without calling 1866 the state's end.
The article dates Abu al-Hasan's temporary burial to 1351 in one section and 1341 in another: no year given.
Article is short (about 500 words); the text uses nearly all of it.

The article gives his death as circa 652 and also as 'the year 652'; the entry says only 7th century, so no year is given. The judgement that the legend's details are untrue comes from the article's unattributed text (old Catholic Encyclopedia wording); attributed here to 'later critics'.
Article is short (about 475 words); the text is about 270 words. 'skandas' is spelled thus in the article; written 'skandhas' here: check if the checker flags it.

The article dates the fall to 'early 614' in its first line and 'by mid-614' later; the text gives no month. The lead says sources vary on whether the city fell without resistance or after a siege; the text follows Sebeos's sequence (submission, revolt, siege) and attributes it to him. Dates for the Christian revolt vary (9 April or 19 May 614, 25 June 615): none given.
Entry says commentaries on all four Vedas; the article says nearly all parts of the Vedas. The text avoids the claim.

The article says Alexander III came to power in 1262 by winning the support of the clansmen; he had in fact been king since 1249 (not stated in the entry). Left out. Short article; text kept near 300 words.

The article says her son died at the age of three and her husband five years later in 1626, but its family list dates Kōchiyo 1619-1621: no age given. Married in 1603 'when seven years old' (East Asian reckoning); age left out.
The article places the division into five regent houses both in the Kamakura period and in the 12th century; no date given.

The entry says he disappeared during a campaign in the south in 1571; the article says he was murdered on the southern frontier in 1571 through a conspiracy of Lord Phya Nakhon and a former abbot of Wat Maximavat. The manner of his end is left out. The article says he took Chiang Saen as his capital in 1548 as king of Lan Na; left out.

Article gives his accession as 609 or 611; the entry says 609. No year given. Article says Shibi supplied Li Yuan with 2,000 horses and 500 cavalry in one place, and 2,000 men and 1,000 horses in another; no figures given. 'Career' used for his support of the rebels; he is a monarch, so 'Reign' covers the first section.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words, and beyond the entry it adds only a few facts (the Pactum Sicardi of 836, Radelchis and Siconulf), too little for 260 words without padding
The lead's 'act of French state-terrorism' is given as the view of David Lange and scholars, as the Aftermath section attributes it.
The article dates the signing to 26 March 1987; the entry says 13 April 1987. No signing date is given in the text. Short article (about 475 words); two sections only.
Entry calls the 1850-1853 war the Eighth Frontier War; the article does not use that name, so the text says only that the rising began in December 1850.
The entry says Paisius was a monk of Hilandar; the article says he finished the book at Zograf after leaving Hilandar. Both are kept as consistent: he began it at Hilandar and finished it at Zograf.

The article places the founding of the Somali Youth Club in Harar in 1943 and later says it opened an office in Mogadishu; the entry says it was founded in Mogadishu. The place of founding is left out. The article dates the renaming to the Somali Youth League 'by 1948', after the Four Power Commission's visit; the entry says 1947. The year of renaming is left out. The 1956 and 1959 elections in the entry are not in the article.

The article does not name the lyricist; the entry names Ri Chan, and that is not repeated. The entry's sentence about Kim Chaek seems garbled; the article does not mention him. A short article: the text uses nearly all of it.

The article's verdict sentence says 'the other fifty received life sentences', evidently a slip; the text does not give the sentences of the other five. Death toll estimates (25,000-50,000 in Singapore) agree with the entry and are not repeated.

The article gives the 1803 armistice as December 1803 and the 1820 coalition as 4 December 1820; the text dates the return to 12 December 1820 as the article does. Zalongo is mentioned in the article only through its later remembrance (the Song of Zalongo, Lela Karagianni's 'women of Zalongo'); not repeated.

The article's own wording is partisan in places ('terrorist attacks', 'the struggle went badly for South Africa's opponents', 'immeasurably superior'); these judgements were left out. The article dates the fall of apartheid to 1991; not used.

The article dates the conquest 1512-1529 (completed by Charles V, the Treaty of Cambrai sealing it); the entry dates it 1512-1524. The text does not give an end date for the conquest as such: it says resistance ended in 1524 and mentions the 1528 withdrawal and the 1529 treaty as aftermath. The entry speaks of attempts to restore John III and Catherine; the 1521 expedition in the article was Henry II's. The text names Henry II for 1521 as the article does.

The article's account of the Aziz affair has inconsistent dates (a 3 April meeting before 23 April, troops surrendering on '19 March' after the 14 April arrest); only 5 April and 21 April, which fit the sequence, are used. The article does not name Makassar as capital; the entry's capital is not repeated.
The article's lead says the statute was the basis of government 'from 1284 until 1536'; the entry gives the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535-1542. The text gives no end date beyond the entry's.

The article gives his birth as 1775 or 1780; the entry c. 1775. No birth year in the text. The entry dates his Moldavian caimacamship 1821-1822; the article gives Wallachia (nominal) in 1821 and Moldavia in 1822. The text gives no year for the Moldavian post. The article does not give 1834 for the Samos appointment; no year given in the text.

The entry says he took the title Herceg of Saint Sava in 1448; the article says he added herceg in the first half of 1448 as Herceg of Hum and the Coast and changed it to Herceg of Saint Sava in late 1449 or early 1450. The text gives no date for the Saint Sava style. Birth 'probably 1404' in the article; the entry's 1404 is not repeated.

The article names the builder of the present building as Carl Wijnbladh (1705-1768), which sits uneasily with the entry's building of 1770; the builder and date are left out. The article's lead says the site 'was moved in the 15th century'; not used.

The article dates the start of the Ladakh expedition both to 1532 and to autumn 1531 (Safar 938 AH); no year is given for the departure. The article does not give 1487 for his birth ('late 15th century'); not repeated.
The entry calls the site 'near Muş'; the article gives about 30 km north-west of Mush, used as given.

The article dates Geumgwan Gaya from 43; the entry dates his traditional reign and birth from 42 CE. No founding year is given in the text. The article does not use the word 'golden egg'; it describes a gold bowl holding six eggs.

The article dates the start to 967/968 (the Danube crossing in August 967 or 968); the entry says 968. No year is given for the crossing. The entry's 972 for Sviatoslav's death is not in the article, which says only that he was killed in a Pecheneg ambush on the Dnieper on his way home; not repeated.
The entry says the cult flourished after the age of the moai; the article says it is unknown whether it replaced the moai-based religion or coexisted with it. The point is left out of the text.
The entry's support for southern African liberation movements is not in the article; not repeated. Present office-holders and 'as of' equipment figures in the article are left out.

The article calls him the fourth khagan and the third son of Bumin; the entry calls Muqan his brother and predecessor, which agrees. The council's objection in the article concerns the mother of the heir; the wording 'his mother' is ambiguous and is read here as Talopien's.

The entry's battle of 761 is not in the article and is not repeated. Population before the war: about 30,000 according to Gilligan; about 40,000 displaced according to Human Rights Watch; both attributed. Mutilation accusations summarized as 'atrocities'.
The article calls him Abuna of Ethiopia in its lead, while another tradition says he declined the office; left out. The entry's preaching in Damot is not described in the article and is not expanded.

The article dates Cylon's attempt to 630 BC; the entry says around 632 BCE. No year is given for it here. The Theagenes of Aristophanes' Peace may be another man of the name; the article places the mention under this Theagenes, so it is kept, without the claim that he was a byword being sharpened further.
The war with Sekhukhune (1876 in the entry) is only touched on in the article, which says his railway plans were thwarted by Sekhukhune, whose lands lay in the path; not repeated here.

The article says he served as lieutenant governor and then governor 'from 1758 to 1774'; the entry dates the governorship 1771 to 1774. Both fit: lieutenant governor from 1758, commission as governor March 1771.

Vahram's chronicle places the emperor's hunting death in the valley of Anazarbus in 1141; the emperor is unnamed there and the year is not printed here. The entry's acceptance of Manuel I's overlordship is not in the article and is not repeated.
The article has no history of the region; the entry's lordships of the House of Reuss are not expanded, so there is no History section.
The article says excavations ended in 2010 and also that 'current excavations' are under Liège; worded as 'later work'. The entry's Assyrian palace paintings are not in the article.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance: a few lines on the village, the mosque of 1156, the 2023 earthquake and the 1995 tentative listing

The article gives birth as 1523/24 and also says he died 'at the age of 86'; the age is left out. The article's Bengal campaign passage is mostly about Man Singh and is muddled (it runs to 1601, after Todar Mal's death); left out apart from the entry's existing mention. The article says he succeeded Khwaja Malik I'timad Khan in 1560; left out as it does not square with the 1570-1580 survey chronology, without a second source.

SKIPPED: article under 300 words, most of it already in the entry (the 1870 coup, the 1871 constitution, the death penalty); too little to add three sections The article says he abolished the death penalty shortly after returning to the presidency on 11 September 1877; the entry dates it to 1882.

The article says the Salian Franks were defeated by Julian c. 358 and given permission to settle 'in the 380s'; the entry has Julian allowing them to stay in 358. The year of the settlement is left out.

The article says the western part was split off in 1513 and transferred to the Polish Crown as the Podlaskie Voivodeship; the transfer to the Crown is not dated in a way that can be checked here, so only the split is given. The article's sentence on 1793 (counties merged into Grodno Voivodeship) is garbled and left out.

The entry says he repelled the first Mongol invasion; the article says the Vietnamese army was routed and Uriyangkhadai left Thang Long after nine days to invade the Song. The reason for the Mongol departure is left out so the page does not contradict itself; the defeats in the field are kept. Accession: the article says 1226 (with the era name Kiến Trung from 1225); the entry has the 1225 marriage. No accession year is printed.

The article says that on Liutprand's death in 744 Transamund regained power and held it for another year under King Hildeprand until his death, and dates his rule 724-745; the entry says he was finally overthrown in 742. The return of 744 is left out. Short article: about 290 words written; nothing added beyond it.
The entry's line on where the border was fixed is not in the article and is not repeated.

The article calls the plebiscite 'deeply flawed' in its own voice; here the specific complaints are given and the judgement attributed loosely to later critics. The entry's 'large majorities' is not contradicted.

The article gives the year of Menelik's denunciation as 1893 in its lead and 1894 later; no year is printed. Article 3's place names in the article are garbled ('From Rafali, Haliy and Segheneiti'); only Segheneiti is named.

The article's lead says the alliance was signed in May 1668 (Sweden's signature, 5 May NS); its body gives 23 January 1668 for England and the Republic, as the entry's January. The text gives only Sweden's 5 May date. The entry's break-up after Charles II's secret alliance with France in 1670 is not in the article; the text says only that England and Sweden backed France in 1672.
Article gives his death as 12 February 1128; the entry says only d. 1128, so the day is left out to keep the text in step with the entry's dates (not a contradiction).

The entry dates the Chikulamayembe dynasty to the late 18th century; the article says Unyamwezi traders were active by the mid-eighteenth century and their leader founded the dynasty, without a firm date. The text gives no date for the founding. Left out the post-1994 regional politics and the assessment of Banda-era exclusion (present-day political judgement).

The entry says he received lands in the western part of the Mongol steppe; the article places his ulus in the Left Wing (eastern portion) of Batu's possessions, east of the Ural Mountains and Ural River. The text does not say where his ulus lay. The Toktemir who attacked Tver' in 1294/1295 is a different person; left out.
Short article (about 320 words); text kept near the lower limit.

The entry says the castle was built in the early 12th century; the article says the first castle was built before 1100 and the second phase, with the keep, dates to 1139/40. The text gives only the keep's date and does not date the first castle. Short article (about 320 words).

Behrend says the victims included Muslim converts; other sources mention only Christians. Left out. The article gives the period of executions as 31 January 1885 to 27 January 1887; the entry says 1885-1887; consistent, days left out.

The article dates the war 1980-1986, counting the West Nile insurgency of autumn 1980 as its start; the entry dates it 1981-1986 (the NRA's rising of 6 February 1981). The text tells the West Nile rising as background and does not call it the start of the war.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance; it also dates the conquest of the Sealand to the second half of the 16th century BC, against the entry's c. 1460 BCE
Short article (about 330 words); written near the lower limit.
Short article (about 480 words); the governors Brooke and Wood and the schools and sanitation named in the entry are not in it.
Left out the NIRF ranking and the NAAC grade (rankings).

The entry's British occupation resisted until 1901 is not dated in the article; the text gives no date. The entry says the ruling house was traced to Benin; the article tells only of resistance to Benin under Oba Ozolua, so no claim on the dynasty's origin is made. The present Onojie (living) is not named.

The entry says Partav was the Albanian capital from the late fifth century; the article says the city was built and made capital in the middle of the 5th century. The text says only 'in the 5th century'. The entry's later drawing of Utik's Christians to the Armenian Church and the Islamisation of the plains are not in the article and are not touched.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance (about 300 words, lyrics sections empty); little beyond the entry
Short article (about 340 words); the gold production and garrisons named in the entry are not in it.

Left out the 'Europe's fifth largest hospital' ranking and the present staff and patient figures. The Time report of March 1938 listing Baumgarten among suicides was wrong (he fled to China); left out.
The article dates Ndiaye's founding to 1287 but also reports Fage (14th century) and Boulegue (c. 1300); all three given as the article gives them. The entry gives no date.

The entry says Raja Wodeyar I took Srirangapatna in 1610; the article's lead says Timmaraja Wodeyar II seized it in 1610, while its History and curse sections give Raja Wodeyar I. The capture is left out. The entry dates Hyder Ali's real power from 1761; the article gives 1766 in its lead and 1760 in History. The period of Hyder Ali and Tipu is left out of the text.
The article dates the Wagri from the ninth to twelfth centuries; the entry says from about the 8th. No starting century given in the text.

The entry lists the Black Budget's taxes as beer, cigarettes and cars; the article gives beer and tobacco in its lead and petrol, cigarettes and beer in the body. The taxes are not listed in the text.

The entry says the town served as seat of government of the Republic of Texas in the 1840s; the article does not mention this and says the leaders favoured Waterloo (Austin) as permanent capital. Left as the entry has it; not repeated. The article says the delegates adopted the declaration on 2 March and signed it the next day; the text says only that they signed it the day after its adoption, so as not to repeat the entry's 2 March.

The entry says the temple is part of the Historic City of Ayutthaya World Heritage Site; the article says it is part of Ayutthaya Historical Park but NOT part of the World Heritage Site. Neither stated in the text; the entry may need checking.
Article dimensions (7.8 by 2.1 km) agree with the entry's 'about 8 kilometres' and 'over 2 kilometres'; not repeated.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance: the film's plot, a 1937 recording, the radio call sign and the dropped Stalin stanza
The article does not give the year he became stadtholder of Friesland (entry: 1584); not stated.
The article's lead says he became prime minister in May 1912, its body that he was sworn in on 10 July 1912; no date given in the text.

The article gives Mount Damota as 2738 m in one place and about 3,000 m in others; no height given. The article's history sections are written in partisan language ('proud people', 'centuries-old oppression'); the text keeps to the dated facts.
The entry says Smolino secured half a century of peace; the article says the peace lasted nearly 60 years, until 1558. The length of the peace is not stated in the text.
The article gives his death as 31 December 501 but also says 'around the new year 501'; no day given in the text.

The article dates his appointment as vizier to 979 in the lead and to 977-78 in the body; no year given in the text. The article's claim that a university was founded at al-Azhar on his instructions is left out as doubtful in its wording.
The article spells the general Yŏn Kaesomun; the text uses Yeon Gaesomun as the entry does. The entry's 'more than a hundred officials' is not in the article and is not repeated.

Article names the founder Yervand IV the Last (220-201 BC); entry calls him Orontes IV. Text uses only Yervand. The article does not mention Artaxias I moving the capital to Artaxata or the modern border; not repeated.
The article's date of death, June 4, 1615 (month-first), is not given in the text.

The article calls Dubdi the oldest monastery in Sikkim and Sikkim's first monastery; the entry says among the oldest, so neither claim is repeated. The article says both that the kingdom was established at Yuksom in 1642 and that Phuntsog moved his capital to Yuksom; the text does not say when the capital was set there.

The article dates his rule as prince 1325-1340 and his succession 1323/1325; the entry gives 1323, so no year of accession is printed. The article gives his death as 7 April 1340; the entry's dates give only 1340, so the day is left out to stay with the entry's level of detail. The entry says Poland and Lithuania divided his realm; the text keeps only the end of independence, as in the article.
Historians disagree on his last Ottoman post (chief of staff of the First Army per Khoury, or of the army in the Caucasus per Roded); left out.

The article says El Cid served Zaragoza until 1086, after al-Mu'taman's death; left out. The article's sentence on the loss of Valencia in 1085 is confused (it describes Toledo being handed over); only Toledo is mentioned.
The article gives his death as 21 or 22 August 1775; the text says only August, as the entry gives the year. The article as given does not describe how he was killed.
The article spells the usurper both Woyanqudi and Woyuanqudi; the first is used.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; beyond the entry it adds only the name's meaning, Fez in 959 and a few details of Ashir. Note: the article dates Ashir to 935, the entry to around 936.

SKIPPED: article too thin: a few sentences beyond the entry, the rest a quoted Amarna letter (EA 60). Note: it places Amurru in southern Syria and cites research that Amurru was a decentralized land Abdi-Ashirta did not directly rule, against the entry's location and wording.

The article dates his rule 1672 to 1686; the entry has 1672 to 1687 (the fall of Golconda and his arrest in 1687). No end year is printed. The entry's eight-month siege of Golconda is not in the article; the text speaks only of the Mughal force led by Aurangzeb's son.

The entry says Chalcis and Megalopolis lost their independence; the article does not name them, and it says some cities, including Athens and Sparta, were later granted autonomy. Neither point is printed.

The article says Adalrich founded Hohenburg (and Ebersheim) and made Odilia its first abbess; the entry says Odile founded the convent of Hohenburg. The text does not say who founded Hohenburg. The article gives his death as 690; the entry has c. 690. No year printed.
The article says the Amoghapasa statue was found at Rambahan, West Sumatra; the entry calls it the statue of Dharmasraya. The place is left out.

The entry calls him military governor of the Philippines in succession to Arthur MacArthur; the article says he commanded American forces there after the military government was dissolved and civil rule instituted under Taft. The text gives only his command and its dates.

SKIPPED: article too thin: about 300 words, half of it a list of children dying in infancy. Doubtful points too: it has King Charles X Gustav making him an offer in 1661 and the posthumous son born eight days after a death on 21 November with a birth date of 30 November; it says Johann Georg inherited Eisenach in 1671, where the entry says it was redistributed among the Ernestine dukes.
The article dates the fortress to the reign of Harold Bluetooth and/or Sweyn Forkbeard; the entry says probably under Harald Bluetooth. The builder is not named in the text.
The article says he remained in Fez during his exile; the entry says he was deported to Marrakesh. The text says only Morocco.
The article gives his death as 5 January 1959 in the lead and 3 January 1959 in the body; the text says only January 1959.
The article also says the capital was moved to Nsachi in the mid-seventeenth century, which sits oddly with Nyanaoase as capital until 1730; left out.
The article dates the Mongols' arrival at Aleppo to December 1259; the entry says they invaded in 1260, so the month is left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words, most of it already in the description (the treaty with Muwatalli II, Appaliuna, the comparison with Alexandros)
The article does not say Perseus died at Alba Fucens (only that he was held there); worded so as not to touch the point.

The entry says the colonial assemblies and the Crown rejected the plan; the article says it was never sent to the Crown, though the Board of Trade (or Colonial Office) rejected it. The Crown's part is left out. The article gives the union as 11 colonies in one place and all the British North American colonies in another; no number given.

The entry says he bought Pesaro in 1445; the article says he obtained the lordship from Galeazzo Malatesta in 1444. The date of the purchase is left out. Costanza's death is given by the article as 1447 while bearing Costanzo, but Battista is dated 1446; birth order not stated.

The article places Alula on the Guardafui Channel; the entry says the Gulf of Aden. The water is not named in the text. The article calls Alula the main capital of the Majeerteen Sultanate; the entry calls it one of the seats of the boqors. Not repeated.
The article says Xenophon describes him as Seuthes I's overlord, apparently a slip for Seuthes II; worded without the numeral. Short article; text kept near 270 words.
The article gives Lama Dorji's death as 13 January 1752 and, from other sources, December 1752; no date given.
The article does not date Teleclus's conquest; the entry's 'probably in the eighth century BCE' is left untouched.
The article's narrative of Dyfed is loosely sourced (Cadell's acquisition of Dyfed is called ambiguous); hedged accordingly.
The article gives al-Mu'tazz's death as 16 July 869 in one place and his murder as 15 July 869 in another; only the month is given.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, much of it quotations; the rest (his wife's name, Beja, a lost coin) would not fill a longer text
The article also calls Ankober the capital of a kingdom of Shewa founded by Yekuno Amlak in the 13th century, which sits badly with Amha Iyasus moving the capital there; left out.

The article says the Apostolic Camera was abolished by Praedicate evangelium as of 5 June 2022; the entry speaks of it in the present tense as governing the Holy See's goods during a vacancy. The abolition is left out; the entry may need updating.

The entry says the quarrel was with his brothers (Herodotus) and that the Libyans defeated him at Leucon; the article's main narrative follows Plutarch (Learchus and his supporters, with Libyans). Told as Plutarch's account, without contradicting Herodotus's version.
The article does not mention Venezuela's help or the runway length; not repeated. Airline lists and incidents left out as liable to change.

The article dates the Battle of Aricia to 508 BCE; the entry says around 504 BCE. The date is left out. Article gives his life as c. 550 - c. 490 BCE; entry dates 'late 6th century BCE'. Death date c. 490 kept as in both.
Left out the article's account of Spínola's later exile activities (ELP, MDLP, Wallraff) as being about Spínola rather than the movement.

The article says Asander had married Dynamis by 47 BCE; the entry places the marriage with his seizure of power. The text does not date the marriage. The article gives his life as 110-17 BC; not repeated.
Article dates the killing to 17 June 656; consistent with the entry's 656.
Left out the article's claim that a Merovingian-period ship burial here is the oldest in the Nordic countries (no detail of which mound).
Kept to the article's sections on name, geography, roads and population; did not repeat the capitals the entry lists.

The article dates the rebellion 1676-1677; the entry dates it 1676 and says it collapsed after Bacon's death in October 1676. The text gives no end date. The entry says Bacon died of disease; the article lead does not give a cause; not repeated.
SKIPPED: article has about 330 words, most already in the entry; a faithful longer text comes to about 220 words

The article dates his kingship of Georgia from 1466; the text says only that he proclaimed himself king after George VIII's capture in 1465, as the entry has it. Article says 'he was succeeded by his son Alexander II' and then that Alexander briefly attempted to claim the throne before being deposed; worded to cover both.
Short article (about 310 words); text kept short rather than padded.
The entry speaks of distinctive village councils; the article does not mention them. Nothing contradicts.

The article identifies him flatly as Giovanni Battista Perasso (1735-1781); the entry says he is usually identified with Perasso and dates him fl. 1746. The lifespan is left out. The article says the stone was thrown at an Austrian official in the lead and at the patrol in the legend; the entry says soldiers. Text uses the patrol.

The article says the raiders came from either Ottoman Algeria or Salé and took between 100 and 237 people; the entry says Algiers and more than a hundred. Neither the origin nor the number is given in the text.

The entry says Makuria received grain, wine and cloth; the article says wheat and lentils. The text says only goods. The entry says the peace lasted about six centuries; the article says almost seven hundred years, and half a millennium. No duration is given in the text.

The article says the Treaty of Vienna confirmed 'the return of the Two Sicilies to Spain'; the entry says the victory made Naples an independent monarchy under a Bourbon dynasty. The text says only that the treaty confirmed the outcome.

The article places the battle near Tarraco and says Cissa may have lain near Lleida; the entry places it north of Tarraco. The text does not locate Cissa. The article speaks of the army of Publius Scipio commanded by Gnaeus; only Scipio is named in the text.
The article is short (about 460 words); the text keeps to what it gives.
The article gives two reasons for Shalva Akhaltsikheli's execution (refusal to renounce Christianity; letters sent from the enemy camp); both are given, attributed to accounts.
The article gives the distance between Huáscar and Esmeralda as 600 meters (660 yards), an inconsistent conversion; distances left out.
The article's line on French losses ("only 11 men killed") is ambiguous and is left out.

The article's lead puts the grounding of the Norwegian ships on the night of 1 October, its narrative on the night of 30 September (refloated and grounded again the next morning); worded without a date. The entry says the Treaty of Perth ceded the Hebrides and Man; the article says they were leased in return for an annual payment. The treaty's terms are left out.
Short article, much of it a long quotation from Roger de Hoveden and a list of novels; the text keeps to the account.
The article gives the date as 5 August 641 or 642 (642 according to Ward; the Annales Cambriae give 644); the entry's 642 is not repeated and no year is given.
The article's lead says September 539 BC; the chronicle's month Tashritu is given as 27 September to 27 October. Only the month name is used.
The article says the Magyars made no further raid on East Francia in Henry's lifetime; the entry says Magyar raids continued until 955. Left out.
The article says contemporary chronicles disagree on how far Máté Csák's forces helped the Abas in the battle itself; the Chronicon Pictum's account of the reinforcement at Sáros is attributed to it.
The article's lead describes the Alamanni as invading Gaul, while its account has Valentinian campaigning beyond the Rhine; the text follows the account, as the entry does.
The article has Grasser predicting a breakthrough 'on 29 June', evidently a slip for July; the date is left out.

Fernández Duro's count of Spanish losses (of 38 ships, twelve beached of which nine refloated, one burned, nine captured, three wrecked) sits uneasily with the entry's 'destroyed most of a large Spanish armada'; only de Boer's figures are given. The entry says the victory ended Spain's attempts to reinforce Flanders by sea; the article says most of the troops and the money reached Flanders. The text gives the Spanish reckoning of troops landed without a judgement.
The entry calls the 4,000 mercenaries Celtiberian; the article calls them Iberian. The text says Iberian only of the troops, without the word Celtiberian.
The article says both that Skanderbeg led twenty-five years of warfare and that the battle opened almost 40 years of war between the League and the Ottomans; neither figure is used.
